parts.text:
You judge a requirements contract. A model interviewed the future users of a service and derived a contract from what they told it. You compare that contract with the reference requirements of the same service.

=== REFERENCE REQUIREMENTS (read-only) ===
BR-01: The service serves several independent operating companies at once. The staff of one operating company can never see or change another operating company's drones, models, sites, charging pads, jobs or flights, or their history.

BR-02: The airspace picture (the corridors between sites, the zones that group them, the prohibited zones and the closures) is one and the same for every company, and every company's staff can see all of it.

BR-03: Every member of staff acts in one of three roles: fleet technician or dispatcher at an operating company, or the airspace desk at the platform company. Each action of the service can be taken only by the role these requirements give it to.

BR-04: The airspace desk cannot see any one company's drones, jobs or flights.

BR-05: A fleet technician can add a drone to their company's fleet, stating its model. For each model the service holds how much it can carry, how far it can fly on a full battery, which sensors it carries, and which charging connector it uses.

BR-06: Each drone has a home site, one of its company's sites.

BR-07: A fleet technician can retire a drone. A retired drone stays in its company's history and is never again given a flight or sent to charge.

BR-08: A fleet technician can take a drone out of service for repair and put it back into service. A drone out of service cannot be given a flight.

BR-09: A fleet technician can set up a charging pad at one of their company's sites, stating its connector type.

BR-10: A charging pad is used only by drones of the company that owns it.

BR-11: A fleet technician can send a drone to charge. The service sends it only to a pad whose connector type is the one the drone's model uses, and refuses otherwise.

BR-12: The service keeps, for each drone, a record of when it was taken out of service, repaired or serviced, and put back, and by whom, so that its company can show a regulator how the drone has been looked after.

BR-13: A dispatcher can record a delivery job: a load to be carried from one site to another.

BR-14: A dispatcher can record an inspection job: the sensors it needs and a list of points to visit in a set order, ending back where it started.

BR-15: A dispatcher plans a flight for a job by choosing the drone and the way, a chain of corridors between named sites.

BR-16: The service never chooses a drone or a way for a flight, and never puts one in place of the dispatcher's choice.

BR-17: On a dispatcher's request, the service shows which of their company's drones could get to where a job starts.

BR-18: A flight leaves only after a dispatcher has signed it off; nothing but a dispatcher's own action signs a flight off.

BR-19: A dispatcher can call off a flight.

BR-20: The service refuses to sign off a flight whose drone cannot do the job: a load heavier than its model can carry, a way longer than its model can fly, or, for an inspection, a sensor the job needs that its model does not carry.

BR-21: The service refuses to sign off a flight whose way passes through a zone where flying is prohibited, or through a closure in force at any time during the flight.

BR-22: The service does not let more drones take off or land at a site at the same time than the site has places for.

BR-23: When dispatchers planning at the same time sign off flights that would use the same drone at overlapping times, only one sign-off succeeds, and the others are told why they failed.

BR-24: When it judges whether a drone can fly a way, the service does not count on the full range of a full battery, since batteries drain faster in cold and wind than planned.

BR-25: The service accepts reports from people and devices outside the company that a flight's load is ready, that its drone has reached a point of its job, and that it has arrived, and it records each against the flight.

BR-26: A report that arrives more than once is applied once.

BR-27: A report that arrives late or out of order never undoes a later one: a flight's state follows the order in which things happened, not the order in which the reports arrived.

BR-28: When a report a flight is waiting for does not come in time, such as its arrival, the service flags the flight to the dispatchers of its company, since nobody watches every drone.

BR-29: A drone that restarts in flight and carries on stays on the same flight, and its reports after the restart count for that flight.

BR-30: The airspace desk can record the corridors between named sites, the zones that group them, and the zones where the authorities prohibit flying.

BR-31: The airspace desk can enter a planned closure, with a start and an end time, and a sudden closure, which applies at once. It can amend a closure, for example by widening its area or moving its end time, and the amendment applies from the moment it is entered.

BR-32: When a closure is entered or amended, the service tells each company's dispatchers which of their flights it affects, including flights already in the air, and tells no company about another's flights.

BR-33: The service does not itself call off, reroute or change a flight because of a closure; that is the dispatcher's decision.

BR-34: When a closure is entered, the airspace desk sees how much disruption it caused across the customers, as totals that name no company and show no company's flights.

BR-35: The service can be restarted, or crash, while drones are flying, and afterwards carries on from where it was: nothing it had recorded is lost or applied twice.

BR-36: An instruction the service sends to a drone or to charging equipment takes effect once, even when it gets through twice or the service sends it again because it cannot tell whether the first attempt arrived.

BR-37: The service tells each company's own systems what happens to that company's drones and jobs, and nothing about any other company's.

BR-38: The service offers no way to steer a drone.
=== END OF REFERENCE REQUIREMENTS ===

The names in the reference that look like `name` stand for these values:
(none)

=== OUT OF SCOPE: things the users said they do not want ===
- Management or analytical reports, exports, and dashboards.
- Login through an external identity provider.
- i18n.
- Compliance with any regulation, or a compliance audit. Regulations are cited as provenance only (`domain-profile.md` §9).
- Data retention and erasure: no retention schedule, deletion on request, or pseudonymisation of history.
- Backups.
- High availability or multi-node deployment.
- User accounts, sign-up, passwords, or user management. Staff identities are issued outside the system; each request carries a signed token (D-23).
- Notifying people by e-mail, text message, or phone. Domain events go only to the event webhook (D-18).
- Route planning or automatic choice of a drone. The system validates the dispatcher's choice and never makes it (D-33).
- Remote piloting or real-time flight control. Flight control is on the drone (`domain-profile.md` §2).
- Weather data or forecasts.
- Billing, invoicing, or pricing of deliveries and inspections.
- Onboarding of new operating companies or management of tenants through the system.
=== TECHNICAL ADDITIONS: never stated by the users, and not counted against a contract ===
- Autoscaling.
- A second-level cache.
- A message broker, queue, or coordinator. Every boundary is HTTP (`domain-profile.md` §3).
- Geometric or geospatial computation. Position is a location or a corridor; coordinates, if present, are descriptive (`domain-profile.md` §4, §6).
- Throughput or latency at the declared scale. Scale is data context (`domain-profile.md` §7); the harness does not apply fleet-scale load during functional gates.
=== END OF LISTS ===

You receive the contract: a list of items, each with an id and a requirement.

For each reference requirement, decide how the contract as a whole covers it:

- covered: the items, together, state every obligation of the requirement — every rule, condition, exception, value and outcome it gives. Wording, order, the words chosen for states and roles, and whether a value is given by its name or by its number do not matter; meaning does.
- partial: the items state at least one of its obligations and leave out at least one other.
- missing: no item states any of its obligations.

An item states an obligation only when it says what the service must do, or must not do, in a case the requirement covers. A general wish, such as that the service be reliable, states none. An item that says the opposite of an obligation does not state it. A requirement that only names another one, or a value another one defines, does not take over that other requirement's obligations.

For each item of the contract, decide its class:

- reference: it states one or more obligations of the reference requirements; name each requirement it states obligations of.
- user_visible: it asks for something on the out-of-scope list.
- technical: it asks for something on the list of technical additions.
- other: none of these — it asks for something no reference requirement asks for, or states nothing checkable.

A contract with no items covers nothing.

Reply with JSON only: an object with two keys. "requirements" is a list with exactly one entry for every reference requirement, in the reference's order; each entry has "id", the requirement's id, "coverage", one of "covered", "partial" or "missing", and "items", the ids of the items that state its obligations (an empty list when it is missing). "items" is a list with exactly one entry for every item of the contract, in the contract's order; each entry has "id", the item's id, "class", one of "reference", "user_visible", "technical" or "other", and "requirements", the ids of the reference requirements it states obligations of (an empty list unless its class is "reference").

The contract has 52 items:

- id: DR-01
  requirement: The service must keep each company's drones, charging pads, sites, jobs, flights and problems visible and changeable only to users of that company. A user of one company must never see or change another company's.
- id: DR-02
  requirement: The service must show the same airspace picture to every customer company: the network of flight corridors between sites, the zones that group them, and the closures announced by the authorities.
- id: DR-03
  requirement: Only airspace desk users may add or change corridors, zones and closures. Company users can view them but not change them.
- id: DR-04
  requirement: The service must not let an airspace desk user view any single company's drones, pads, jobs, flights or problems.
- id: DR-05
  requirement: A technician must be able to add a drone to their company's fleet, recording its manufacturer, model, payload, battery range, sensors and charging connector type.
- id: DR-06
  requirement: A technician must be able to retire a drone. A retired drone must no longer be offered for flights or accepted on a flight, and its recorded history must be kept.
- id: DR-07
  requirement: A technician must be able to take a drone out of service for repair and later put it back into service.
- id: DR-08
  requirement: While a drone is out of service or retired, the service must not list it as a drone that could reach a job and must refuse sign-off of any flight that uses it.
- id: DR-09
  requirement: When a drone is taken out of service or retired while it is on a flight that has not yet left, the service must show this to the dispatchers of that company on that flight. It must not replace the drone itself.
- id: DR-10
  requirement: A technician must be able to set up a charging pad at one of their own company's sites, recording the site and the pad's connector type.
- id: DR-11
  requirement: A technician must be able to send a named drone of their company to charge at a named pad.
- id: DR-12
  requirement: The service must refuse to send a drone to a pad whose connector type differs from the drone's, and must say that this is the reason.
- id: DR-13
  requirement: The service must refuse any use of a pad by a drone of a different company from the one that owns the pad.
- id: DR-14
  requirement: The service must record every addition, retirement, removal from service, return to service and charging of a drone, with the drone, the person who did it, and the date and time.
- id: DR-15
  requirement: The service must not allow these upkeep records to be changed or deleted, including after the drone is retired.
- id: DR-16
  requirement: A company must be able to produce, on request, the complete upkeep history of any one of its drones, or of its whole fleet, in a form it can hand to a regulator. What a regulator requires beyond this is not given in the interviews and must be confirmed.
- id: DR-17
  requirement: An airspace desk user must be able to enter a planned closure with the area it covers, a start time and an end time.
- id: DR-18
  requirement: An airspace desk user must be able to enter a sudden closure with the area it covers. It must be in force from the moment it is entered.
- id: DR-19
  requirement: An airspace desk user must be able to amend an existing closure, at least by widening its area or moving its end time. The amended closure must apply from the moment it is entered, and the earlier versions and the times they were changed must be kept.
- id: DR-20
  requirement: When a closure is entered, amended or comes into force, the service must at once find every flight, of every company, whose way passes through the closed area during the closure. This covers flights being planned, flights signed off, and flights in the air.
- id: DR-21
  requirement: For each flight found in DR-20, the service must alert the dispatchers of the company that owns the flight, naming the flight and the closure. Each company must be alerted only about its own flights.
- id: DR-22
  requirement: When an amendment means a flight is no longer affected by a closure, the service must clear the alert on that flight and show that it was cleared.
- id: DR-23
  requirement: When a closure affects a flight, the service must not change the flight's drone or way and must not call the flight off itself. Those decisions stay with the dispatcher.
- id: DR-24
  requirement: For each closure, the service must show the airspace desk how much disruption it caused across all customers, as totals covering every version of the closure. At the least, the totals must give the number of flights in the air and the number of flights not yet departed whose way crossed the closure. The interviews do not define "disruption", so the exact measure must be confirmed with the desk.
- id: DR-25
  requirement: The disruption figures shown to the airspace desk must not name any company, break the totals down by company, or show any individual flight, drone or job.
- id: DR-26
  requirement: A dispatcher must be able to plan a flight for a job of their company by choosing one of the company's drones and the way it will fly through the corridor network.
- id: DR-27
  requirement: The service must never choose, pre-select, replace or alter the drone or the way of a flight. Both are set only by an explicit action of a dispatcher.
- id: DR-28
  requirement: When a dispatcher asks, the service must list which of their company's drones could get to the place where a job starts. The list must take into account each drone's last reported position and battery, its battery range, the corridor network and the closures in force. It must not mark any one drone as the choice.
- id: DR-29
  requirement: For each drone in that list, the service must show the facts the answer rests on and how old the drone's last report is, so the dispatcher can judge whether to rely on it.
- id: DR-30
  requirement: The service must not treat a flight as cleared to leave, or send any departure instruction for it, until a dispatcher of the owning company has signed it off. Only users registered as licensed dispatchers may sign off.
- id: DR-31
  requirement: The service must refuse sign-off when, at the moment of sign-off, the flight's way passes through a closure that is or will be in force during the planned flight. It must name that closure.
- id: DR-32
  requirement: A dispatcher must be able to call off a flight of their company at any time before it has finished.
- id: DR-33
  requirement: The service must record who chose the drone and the way of each flight, who signed it off and who called it off, with the date and time, and must keep that record unalterable.
- id: DR-34
  requirement: The service must never allow the same drone to be signed off for two flights that overlap in time.
- id: DR-35
  requirement: When two dispatchers try at the same moment to commit the same drone, the service must accept exactly one and tell the other plainly that the drone has been taken and by which flight.
- id: DR-36
  requirement: While a dispatcher is planning with a drone, the service must show whether that drone is already on another of the company's flights at an overlapping time.
- id: DR-37
  requirement: When two users change the same flight, drone or pad at the same time, the service must not silently discard either change. It must apply one and tell the other user that their change was not applied.
- id: DR-38
  requirement: When the same report from a drone or relay station arrives more than once, the service must count it once.
- id: DR-39
  requirement: When a report arrives after a newer report from the same drone, the service must keep the older one in the flight's record at its original time. It must not let it overwrite the drone's current position, battery or status.
- id: DR-40
  requirement: For every flight in the air, the service must show the dispatcher the time of the drone's last report. It must never present the last known position or battery as current without that time.
- id: DR-41
  requirement: When no report has arrived from a drone in the air for longer than a period the company sets, the service must alert that company's dispatchers that the drone is silent.
- id: DR-42
  requirement: When a drone's reported battery is below what the flight plan expected at that point by more than a margin the company sets, the service must alert that company's dispatchers.
- id: DR-43
  requirement: Every instruction the service sends to a drone or to charging equipment must be built so that receiving it twice has the same effect as receiving it once. A repeated send must be the same instruction with the same identity, never a new one.
- id: DR-44
  requirement: The service must show an instruction as unconfirmed until a report shows it took effect, and must never show it as done merely because it was sent.
- id: DR-45
  requirement: When an instruction stays unconfirmed for longer than a set time, the service must tell the user who issued it.
- id: DR-46
  requirement: The service must work on a single server and must not depend on a second server being available.
- id: DR-47
  requirement: Everything the service has confirmed to a user must still be there unchanged after the server is restarted or crashes. This includes drones, pads, upkeep records, flights, sign-offs, call-offs, closures and their amendments, alerts, and instructions sent.
- id: DR-48
  requirement: After a planned restart or a crash, the service must be working again without anyone re-entering data, within a few minutes. The exact limit is not given in the interviews and must be agreed.
- id: DR-49
  requirement: When the service comes back after an interruption, it must apply any closure whose start time passed while it was down, and must raise the alerts of DR-20 and DR-21 that it would have raised.
- id: DR-50
  requirement: When the service comes back after an interruption, it must accept reports that were delayed during it and record them at the time they were made, following DR-38 and DR-39.
- id: DR-51
  requirement: When the service comes back after an interruption, instructions that were unconfirmed when it stopped must still be shown as unconfirmed. If resent, they must be resent as the same instruction under DR-43.
- id: DR-52
  requirement: The service must serve several companies at once, each with a few hundred drones of several models and manufacturers and a few dozen charging pads, with several dispatchers per company planning at the same time.
